summary: Static RLS defines fixed DAX filter rules per role in Power BI Desktop. Each role has one or more table filter expressions. Users assigned to a role see only rows matching those filters.
keyInsight: RLS is enforced in Power BI Service after publishing. RLS does NOT apply to workspace Admins, Members, or Contributors — they always see all data regardless of role assignments.
commonTrap: Thinking RLS applies to workspace members. Only users accessing data through Apps or as workspace Viewers have RLS enforced. Higher workspace roles bypass it entirely.

miniQuiz.question: A user is a Workspace Member and is also assigned to an RLS role filtered to the East region only. What data will they see?
choices: Only the East region — the RLS role restricts their view
All data — workspace Members bypass RLS
No data — RLS blocks all access for Members
Whichever is more restrictive — RLS or workspace role
miniQuiz.explanation: Workspace Admins, Members, and Contributors bypass RLS — they see all data regardless of role assignments. RLS only restricts Viewers or users accessing data through Apps.

summary: Dynamic RLS uses the current user's identity to filter data at runtime. The standard pattern matches [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() against a user-to-data mapping table.
keyInsight: Dynamic RLS requires a user-mapping table in the model. It scales to any number of users with a single role — adding a new user only requires adding a row to the mapping table.
commonTrap: Creating one static RLS role per user. With many users, static roles are unmanageable and require model republishing every time the user list changes.

miniQuiz.question: A company has 200 salespeople, each seeing only their own region's data. What is the most scalable RLS approach?
choices: Create 200 static RLS roles — one per salesperson
Create a user-mapping table and one dynamic RLS role using USERPRINCIPALNAME()
Create one role per region (10 regions = 10 roles)
Use sensitivity labels to restrict data access per user
miniQuiz.explanation: Dynamic RLS with a user-mapping table and USERPRINCIPALNAME() creates one role that automatically filters each user's data. New salespeople are added by inserting a row into the mapping table — no model changes needed.

summary: Power BI workspace roles in order of permission: Admin (full control), Member (publish, edit, manage access), Contributor (publish, edit), Viewer (read-only, RLS enforced).
keyInsight: Only the Viewer role enforces RLS. For broad, RLS-restricted read-only distribution to many users, publish an App — App audience members get Viewer-equivalent access with RLS applied.
commonTrap: Giving users Member or Contributor roles when they only need to view. These roles bypass RLS and expose all underlying data. Use Viewer or App distribution instead.

miniQuiz.question: You want 500 employees to view reports with RLS applied. What is the most appropriate distribution method?
choices: Add all 500 as Workspace Members
Add all 500 as Workspace Viewers
Publish an App and add the 500 employees as the App audience
Share individual reports with each employee
miniQuiz.explanation: Publishing an App and assigning users as the audience gives them viewer-level access with RLS enforced. It also provides a clean, managed distribution experience without exposing the workspace directly.

summary: Sensitivity labels (from Microsoft Purview) classify and protect Power BI content. Labels like Confidential or Highly Confidential can restrict sharing, export, and downstream use of data.
keyInsight: Sensitivity labels propagate downstream — when data is exported to Excel, the label follows it. This ensures protection outside of Power BI. Labels are configured in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal.
commonTrap: Thinking sensitivity labels enforce data access control (who can view). Labels classify and protect data after access — they do not restrict who can view a report. That is handled by workspace roles and RLS.

miniQuiz.question: An organization wants to prevent employees from exporting a dataset containing PII to unprotected Excel files. Which feature addresses this?
choices: Row-Level Security
Workspace Viewer role
Sensitivity labels with export restrictions
Disabled scheduled refresh
miniQuiz.explanation: Sensitivity labels can restrict export actions on classified content. A 'Highly Confidential' label prevents export to unprotected files or requires encryption when exported, protecting PII outside Power BI.

summary: An on-premises data gateway bridges Power BI Service to data sources inside an organizational network. Required for scheduled refresh of on-premises sources (SQL Server, Oracle, files, etc.).
keyInsight: Standard gateway supports multiple users and DirectQuery — required for enterprise use. Personal gateway is single-user only. Cloud sources (Azure SQL, SharePoint Online) do NOT need a gateway.
commonTrap: Assuming all data sources need a gateway. Gateways are only required for on-premises sources or sources within private VNets — not for cloud services.

miniQuiz.question: A scheduled refresh of a report connected to an on-premises SQL Server is failing. What is most likely missing?
choices: A Premium capacity license
An on-premises data gateway configured and running
A DirectQuery connection instead of Import
A certified dataset endorsement
miniQuiz.explanation: Scheduled refresh of on-premises SQL Server requires an on-premises data gateway to bridge the connection between Power BI Service (cloud) and the on-premises network. Without a gateway, refresh will always fail.

summary: Scheduled refresh automatically updates imported datasets on a defined schedule. Requires: dataset credentials configured, a gateway for on-premises sources, and a license within refresh frequency limits.
keyInsight: Pro license: up to 8 refreshes per day. Premium / Fabric: up to 48 refreshes per day. DirectQuery and DirectLake datasets do NOT use scheduled refresh — they query live data.
commonTrap: Expecting DirectQuery datasets to benefit from scheduled refresh. DirectQuery always queries the live source — there is no cached data to refresh.

miniQuiz.question: A Pro license user wants their Import mode dataset to refresh 10 times per day. What is the limitation?
choices: Pro license supports up to 8 refreshes per day — 10 requires Premium or Fabric capacity
Pro license supports unlimited scheduled refreshes
Import mode does not support scheduled refresh at all
Scheduled refresh requires a DirectQuery connection
miniQuiz.explanation: Power BI Pro limits scheduled refresh to 8 times per day. For 10+ daily refreshes, Premium Per User, Premium capacity, or Fabric is required — those support up to 48 refreshes per day.

summary: Endorsement labels mark datasets, reports, or dataflows as trustworthy. Promoted means the content owner vouches for it. Certified requires admin-level verification and carries the highest trust signal.
keyInsight: Certified content is the authoritative signal for organizational data assets. It appears prominently in dataset search and Lineage View, encouraging analysts to reuse governed datasets.
commonTrap: Confusing Promoted with Certified. Any dataset owner can Promote their content. Only authorized certifiers (configured by admins) can Certify — it is a formal governance checkpoint.

miniQuiz.question: A data team wants their master dataset to appear as the authoritative source for all reports across the company. Which endorsement level is most appropriate?
choices: Promoted — the owner can apply this themselves
Certified — requires admin verification and signals the highest organizational trust
Sensitivity label — Confidential
Featured — highlighted on the home experience
miniQuiz.explanation: Certified is the highest endorsement level. It signals organizational trust, appears in dataset search results and Lineage View, and encourages analysts to build on this authoritative, governed dataset.

summary: Deployment pipelines manage Power BI content lifecycle across Development, Test, and Production workspaces. Changes are promoted stage-by-stage with comparison views to see differences before deploying.
keyInsight: Deployment pipelines require Premium or Fabric capacity. They are the recommended ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) approach — ensuring changes are validated before reaching production users.
commonTrap: Manually copying PBIX files between workspaces as a deployment process. This is error-prone and does not preserve dataset configurations or data source settings. Deployment pipelines handle this automatically.

miniQuiz.question: An organization wants to test report changes in a staging environment before publishing to production. Which feature supports this workflow?
choices: Workspace roles with Contributor permissions for staging
Deployment pipelines with Development, Test, and Production stages
Scheduled refresh across multiple workspaces
Sensitivity labels with staged deployment rules
miniQuiz.explanation: Deployment pipelines provide a structured Dev → Test → Production promotion workflow with side-by-side comparison views, ensuring changes are validated before reaching production users.

summary: Dynamic RLS uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() to return the signed-in user's identity (email format, e.g., user@domain.com) and matches it against a security mapping table to determine what data the user can see. One role serves all users.
keyInsight: The UPN format must exactly match the mapping table — case-insensitive in most deployments but case-sensitive in some. Common pitfalls: alias vs. primary UPN, domain suffixes (user@contoso.com vs user@contoso.onmicrosoft.com), and email casing differences. Use LOWER() on both sides when in doubt.
commonTrap: Not testing RLS with the View As feature before publishing. A developer can test their own UPN correctly but miss that other users' UPNs are formatted differently in the mapping table. Always use View As Roles with specific email addresses to validate all user scenarios.

miniQuiz.question: An RLS filter `[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()` is configured. A user reports seeing no data. Their Power BI login is 'jane.doe@company.com' but the mapping table stores 'JaneDoe@COMPANY.COM'. What is the fix?
choices: Change the RLS filter to use USERNAME() instead of USERPRINCIPALNAME()
Update the filter to LOWER([Email]) = LOWER(USERPRINCIPALNAME()) to make the comparison case-insensitive
Create a static RLS role specifically for this user
Add the user as a workspace Admin to bypass RLS
miniQuiz.explanation: Applying LOWER() to both sides of the comparison makes the UPN match case-insensitive. This is the standard fix when email addresses are stored with inconsistent casing in the mapping table. Adding as workspace Admin (D) would bypass RLS entirely — a security violation.

summary: Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview classify Power BI content and follow data outside Power BI. When a dataset is labelled 'Confidential', reports built from it inherit the label automatically (downstream inheritance). Exported files also carry the label.
keyInsight: Sensitivity labels do NOT control who can VIEW a report — that is workspace roles and RLS. Labels control what happens TO the data after access: can it be exported, printed, forwarded? 'Highly Confidential' can encrypt exported Excel files and prevent forwarding.
commonTrap: Expecting sensitivity labels to prevent unauthorized access to reports. Labels are a DATA PROTECTION tool (what happens to data after access), not an ACCESS CONTROL tool (who can see the report). Use workspace roles and RLS for access control. Use labels for compliance and export restrictions.

miniQuiz.question: A compliance requirement states all Power BI reports containing PII must be labelled 'Confidential' and the label must apply automatically when a new report is built from the PII dataset. Which feature enables this?
choices: Configure row-level security on the PII dataset
Enable downstream label inheritance so reports built from the labelled dataset automatically inherit the Confidential label
Require workspace Admins to manually apply labels to each new report
Enable report-level export restrictions in workspace settings
miniQuiz.explanation: Downstream label inheritance propagates the dataset's sensitivity label to all reports, dashboards, and exported files derived from it — automatically, without manual action. This is the scalable compliance enforcement mechanism for Power BI + Microsoft Purview integration.

concept: External Sharing and Azure AD B2B
summary: Power BI can share content with external users (outside the organization) via Azure Active Directory B2B guest invitations. External users access content through Power BI Apps or direct share links. Licensing requirements depend on whether a Premium capacity is used.
keyInsight: External users need a Power BI Pro license OR the content must be in a Premium capacity workspace. In Premium capacity, external B2B guests can consume content without their own Pro license — the capacity license covers consumption. This is the cost-effective model for external distribution.
commonTrap: Attempting to add external users as workspace members without a Premium capacity. Without Premium, every external user needs their own Pro license. The cost-effective solution for many external viewers is a Premium capacity workspace with an App distributed to B2B guest accounts.

miniQuiz.question: A company wants 50 external partners to access Power BI reports. The partners do not have Power BI licenses. What is the most appropriate solution?
choices: Purchase 50 Power BI Pro licenses for the external partners
Export reports to PDF and email them to the partners monthly
Publish the reports to a Premium capacity workspace and invite the external users as Azure AD B2B guests to consume via a Power BI App
Enable public access on the workspace so partners can access without logging in
miniQuiz.explanation: Premium capacity workspaces allow Azure AD B2B guest users to consume Power BI Apps without per-user Pro licenses — the Premium capacity license covers consumption. This is the standard external distribution model for many external viewers. Public access (D) removes all security controls.

concept: Power BI App Permissions and Audiences
summary: Power BI Apps provide a curated, managed view of workspace content to consumers. Apps support audience segments — different users or groups can see different content within the same app. Apps separate workspace content from consumer-facing content.
keyInsight: App audiences allow the same app to show different reports to different groups without separate workspaces or reports. For example, a Sales App with two audiences: North Managers see North reports; South Managers see South reports. RLS provides row-level restriction; audiences provide report-level visibility.
commonTrap: Confusing workspace access with App access. Workspace members (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) see the full workspace and all content in development. App audience members see only what is published to the App — a curated, consumer-friendly subset. Always distribute broadly via Apps, not workspace Viewer roles.

miniQuiz.question: A Sales App should show North team reports to North managers and South team reports to South managers — from the same workspace. How is this configured?
choices: Create two separate workspaces — one per region
Configure App audience segments: one audience for North (with North reports) and one for South (with South reports)
Use row-level security to restrict each manager's report view
Create separate Apps — one per region
miniQuiz.explanation: App audience segments allow one App to serve different content to different groups. North managers are added to the North audience (which includes only North reports); South managers to the South audience. RLS then handles data row restrictions within those reports.

summary: Object-Level Security restricts access to entire tables or specific columns in a semantic model. Users subject to OLS cannot see the restricted column or table anywhere in reports — it appears as if the column/table does not exist.
keyInsight: OLS complements RLS: RLS restricts ROWS (which data records a user sees), OLS restricts COLUMNS or TABLES (which fields are even visible). OLS is configured using Tabular Editor or SQL Server Management Studio — it cannot be configured in Power BI Desktop alone.
commonTrap: Using sensitivity labels when OLS is needed. Sensitivity labels protect data classification and export behavior — they do not hide specific columns from users. OLS is required when a user should not be able to see a column at all (e.g., salary, SSN, credit card number).

miniQuiz.question: HR reports must hide the Salary column from all non-HR users — they should not be able to see or use this column in any report. Which feature implements this?
choices: Row-level security filtering salary rows
Sensitivity label 'Highly Confidential' on the Salary column
Object-Level Security restricting access to the Salary column
Removing the Salary column from all reports manually
miniQuiz.explanation: Object-Level Security hides columns from unauthorized users at the semantic model level — the column does not appear in field lists, cannot be used in visuals or DAX measures, and is invisible to restricted users. RLS restricts rows, not columns. Removing from reports leaves the column in the model where it could be accessed by report builders.

summary: The on-premises data gateway acts as a secure bridge between Power BI Service (cloud) and on-premises data sources. It encrypts all credentials and communication. Gateways run as a Windows service and require a machine that remains always-on for scheduled refresh.
keyInsight: Standard (enterprise) gateway supports multiple users, datasets, and DirectQuery connections — required for enterprise deployments. Personal gateway only supports one user and no DirectQuery. Cloud sources (Azure SQL, SharePoint Online, Azure Data Lake) do NOT need a gateway.
commonTrap: Assuming all data connections require a gateway. Gateways are ONLY required for on-premises sources or sources within private networks (VNets). Azure SQL Database, SharePoint Online, and other cloud services connect directly from the Power BI Service without a gateway.

miniQuiz.question: A semantic model uses three sources: on-premises SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, and SharePoint Online. Which sources require an on-premises data gateway for scheduled refresh?
choices: All three sources require a gateway
Only the on-premises SQL Server requires a gateway
Only Azure SQL Database and SharePoint Online require gateways — cloud sources need them
None — Power BI Service connects directly to all sources
miniQuiz.explanation: Only the on-premises SQL Server requires a gateway — it is behind the corporate network and Power BI Service cannot reach it directly. Azure SQL Database and SharePoint Online are cloud services accessible directly from Power BI Service. Gateways bridge the gap between cloud (Power BI Service) and on-premises networks only.
